analysis.title: China 2027 Outlook: Less Drag, More Uncertainty
key_insights: GS expects China real GDP growth of 4.5% in 2027, down slightly from 4.6% in 2026, consistent with a possible government target of 'around 4.5%'. The forecast does not rely on significant policy easing or a property turnaround.

The baseline rests on smaller growth drags. The property drag on real GDP is expected to narrow from 1.8pp in 2026 to 1.3pp in 2027, and fiscal tightening should subtract about 0.5pp less. Together they give roughly a 1pp lift relative to 2026.

GS sees 2027 uncertainty rising. Risks include US-China relations becoming less stable after four Trump-Xi meetings in 2026, AI capex and tech risks, and the 21st Party Congress in the second half of 2027, which could bring intensified anti-corruption efforts, security restrictions and government risk aversion.

Versus consensus, GS growth (4.5%) is slightly above Bloomberg's 4.4%. GS 2027 CPI (0.5%) is well below Bloomberg and IMF (1.4-1.5%). GS current account surplus (4.9% of GDP) is above IMF (4.0%) and Bloomberg (3.6%). These underpin views of lower rates and a stronger CNY.

The official 2026 GDP figure looks high relative to alternative measures. Real retail sales grew under 2% y/y and real FAI fell about 10% y/y in the first nine months. GS import-implied GDP growth was 2.4% y/y in Q1-Q3 2026, and property, exports and fiscal changes imply a slowdown 1.2pp steeper than the official data.

Exports rose 21.3% y/y in USD terms in Jan-Sep 2026, with export prices up 11% (AI-related products, chip-embedded electronics) and volumes up 9.5%, led by EVs, batteries, solar and electrical equipment. GS expects nominal export growth to slow from 22.9% in 2026 to 13.7% in 2027, and real export growth from 8.5% to 6.0%.

A tougher EU trade stance is a key export risk. The EU is 14% of China's nominal exports and contributed about 2pp to export volume growth in Jan-Sep. GS assumes mutual interests limit escalation, and curbs could shift China toward localizing production in Europe, which would sustain intermediate-input exports such as batteries.

GS forecasts the current account surplus rising from 4.4% of GDP in 2026 to 4.9% in 2027, with the goods trade surplus at 6.0% then 6.3% of GDP. Broad balance of payments is expected to improve from 2.9% to 3.5% of GDP, consistent with gradual CNY appreciation.

The property downturn is in its sixth year. Housing indicators are down 60-90% from 2020-21 peaks, and property's GDP share fell from about 30% to about 15% in 2025, heading to about 8% from 2030. Prices may recover first in top-tier cities such as Shanghai and Shenzhen, while lower-tier cities may keep falling for years. Property investment keeps contracting at double-digit rates.

The labor market is weak, with social insurance enforcement raising labor costs and high-tech sectors less labor-intensive than property and services. GS expects no major effective income policies beyond incremental measures, so the labor market stays weak in 2027.

Household consumption: nominal retail sales of consumer goods grew 1.1% y/y in Q1-Q3 2026 versus 4.5% a year earlier. Trade-in funding fell from RMB300bn to RMB250bn and the NEV purchase tax rose from 0% to 5%, so auto sales fell 14.9%. GS sees real household consumption at 4.2% in 2027 (4.0% in 2026) and retail sales growth at 2.0% (1.0%). The NEV tax rises to 10% in early 2028, which may pull purchases into Q4 2027.

Services consumption is the best growth source. Services retail sales grew 5.0% y/y in Q1-Q3 2026, about 4pp faster than goods. Services are 46% of household spending versus about 60% in the US and Japan. The household savings rate rose to 33.4% in Q3, and deposits keep growing.

Investment: FAI fell 7.2% y/y so far in 2026 after a 3.8% decline in 2025. Crude steel output fell 2.9% and cement 8.6% in the first nine months. GS expects FAI to improve from about -6% in 2026 to about -3% in 2027, and GFCF growth to rise from 2.0% to 2.5%. The 'Six Networks' initiative (RMB28.4tn in the 15th FYP versus RMB24.9tn in the 14th) will not reverse the falling investment share of GDP.

Inflation: PPI turned positive in March 2026 after 41 months of decline and reached 5.7% y/y in October on oil prices (Iran war) and AI hardware prices. Headline CPI was 0.7% and core 0.8% in October. GS expects PPI of 0.3% in 2027 (2.9% in 2026), possibly negative as early as Q2 2027, CPI of 0.5% (0.8%), and core CPI of 0.6% (1.0%), with Brent averaging $88/bbl in 2027.

Monetary policy: on 31 October the PBOC moved its policy rate from the 7-day to the overnight reverse repo rate (1.25%, effective 2 Nov) with a 1.0-1.5% corridor, which GS views as equal to a 5-10bp cut in front-end interbank rates. GS expects one 10bp cut in Q4 2027, after the Party Congress and after the Fed resumes cuts in December 2027, taking the rate to 1.15%.
TSF stock growth is expected to slow from 8.3% at end-2025 to 7.2% at end-2026 and 6.2% at end-2027, as government bond quotas shrink and private credit demand stays weak.

Fiscal: the augmented fiscal deficit fell from 11.4% of GDP in 2025 to 10.0% in 2026 (12-month average hit 9.4% in September, lowest since Oct 2015) and is projected at 9.5% in 2027. The 2026 tightening subtracted 1.1pp from growth. Recent easing (extra RMB550bn local bond quota, RMB800bn new policy-based financial instrument) is seen as short-lived, aimed at securing early-2027 momentum before the March Two Sessions.

Local government funding should worsen. Land sales revenue is expected to fall another 20% in 2027 after a 30% drop in 2026, debt resolution funding drops from RMB2.8tn a year (2024-26) to RMB800bn a year (2027-28), and the mid-2027 LGFV exit deadline adds pressure. Anti-corruption scrutiny continues to limit officials' willingness to launch projects.

Risks to 2027 growth tilt slightly to the downside: renewed US-China tensions, trade barriers (especially Europe), a deeper property contraction, local government financial stress and weak policy implementation. Upside risks are faster exports, stronger AI capex and bigger stimulus, though stimulus would likely follow a shock such as an export slowdown, credit events or social instability.

Market view: GS is overweight China equities into 2027, with equity strategists expecting mid-to-high teen returns. AI hardware profit growth should slow while AI application and internet earnings could rebound from a low base. Heavy positioning in AI hard-tech points to choppy liquidity and sentiment in early 2027, so strategists favor alpha over beta and diversification within the Chinese AI ecosystem.

Rates view: long-end China government bond yields should trend lower in 2027 on subdued demand, weak inflation, slowing credit and lower bond supply. A possible 25% corporate income tax on government bond interest could lift yields once as a one-off step.

FX view: GS forecasts USD/CNY at 6.60 / 6.50 / 6.30 in 3 / 6 / 12 months, faster than forward pricing, on the widening goods surplus (US$1.3tn in 2026, US$1.5tn in 2027), exporter FX conversion (66% in September) and RMB internationalization. The PBOC doubled the FX deposit reserve requirement ratio from 2% to 4% to slow appreciation, and Beijing is seen favoring about 3-5% a year.

Hong Kong: real GDP grew 5.2% y/y in Q3 2026 (5.1% year to date) on finance and trade, with H1 financial activities up 7.6% and IPO fundraising of HK$388bn in nine months. GS expects growth to slow to 3.1% in 2027 from 5.0% in 2026, residential price growth to slow from 15% to 7%, and CPI at 1.7% (1.8% in 2026).

risk_factors: Renewed US-China tensions, including expiry of the tariff and rare earth pause on 10 Jan 2027.
Significant trade barriers from other major partners, especially the EU.
Rising financial stress among local governments and LGFVs, with the mid-2027 LGFV exit deadline.
Weak policy implementation and local officials lacking incentives under anti-corruption scrutiny.
21st Party Congress effects: anti-corruption, security restrictions and risk aversion.
Weak sentiment and a labor market where strong industrial output does not translate into jobs or household income.
Persistent weak domestic demand could become a structural downtrend in household consumption growth.
Heavy positioning in AI hard-tech equities.
Hong Kong: moderating IPO activity, Fed rate hikes and US-China technology tensions.
vol_and_positioning: Investor positioning in Chinese AI hard-tech equities is still heavy, pointing to a choppy liquidity and sentiment backdrop in early 2027.
GS strategists reiterate an alpha-over-beta strategy and diversification within the Chinese AI ecosystem.
geopolitical: US-China relations may become less stable in 2027 after four Trump-Xi meetings kept tensions in check in 2026.
An extended tariff and rare earth control pause agreed at the Trump-Xi meeting in Washington expires 10 Jan 2027.
A tougher EU trade stance toward China is a key export risk. China holds leverage through rare earths, and EU-China trade talks continue.
The 21st Party Congress in autumn 2027 could bring intensified anti-corruption efforts, security restrictions and government risk aversion.
Higher oil prices from the Iran war and the most severe oil supply shock in decades lifted China's PPI in 2026.
G20 summit in Miami on 14-15 Dec 2026 and APEC in Shenzhen on 18-19 Nov 2026 are listed as upcoming catalysts.
Renewed US-China technology tensions are a downside risk to Hong Kong capital markets.

tension_points.bull_case: Smaller property and fiscal drags give roughly a 1pp lift versus 2026, exports stay resilient (real growth 6.0%) and services consumption keeps growing, supporting 4.5% GDP growth.
tension_points.bear_case: Official GDP looks high versus alternative measures (real retail sales under 2%, real FAI down about 10%, import-implied GDP 2.4%). Weak sentiment, jobs and local government finances, US-China and EU trade risks, and Party Congress risk aversion could undercut growth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Renewed US-China tensions when the tariff and rare earth pause expires 10 Jan 2027, or a deeper property contraction or local government credit event.

tension_points.bull_case: Manufacturing competitiveness and ample capacity support market share gains, especially in emerging markets, with real export growth of 5-6% over the next few years.
tension_points.bear_case: A tougher EU trade stance could cut exports (the EU is 14% of nominal exports) and nominal growth slows as chip and oil prices ease.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Significant new EU trade barriers on Chinese goods.
